The record’s summary, whole

The 4.0.0 release plan addresses issues filed by this repository and by adopters. The original 2026-10-12 scope covered 26 issues against CodeFlow 3.0.0 and 3.1.0. The combined scope covers codeflow ci verdicts that depend on how a range is spelled, planning and exemption pull requests that cannot be classified, guards that miss commands, writers and history reads that can be redirected in a local clone, CodeFlow's own pushes using a personal credential, managed CI steps an adopter must edit by hand, a landing mode, tests that touch an enclosing repository, and one post-release evaluation. This epic fixes or settles each of them for the 4.0.0 release, which the operator renumbered from 3.2.0 on 2026-10-28 (Version relabel amendment below).

Done means

each task below has landed on integration/EPC-022-the-3-2-0-milestone-fixes with its cross-lineage review, the integrated body passes the full gate and the journey below on the installed candidate, and its pull request to main is ready for a human merge.

The record’s summary, whole

Five feature requests from adopters in October 2026 ask CodeFlow to change its defaults rather than fix a defect: a define-once gate with a tracked exemption register (issue 274), strict typing and linting by default with an explicit opt-out (275), a repository that holds only what it needs long term (279), a local run of the managed secret scan and dependency audit (252), per-project account profiles with limit-aware seat routing (234), and the supervisor and separate-account layers of lane isolation (286, items 2 and 3; item 1 is TSK-437 in 4.0.0). The operator placed them on 2026-10-22 in one separate epic, smaller than EPC-022, sized by issue 280's guidance; this epic is that placement.

Done means

each task has landed on this epic's line with its cross-lineage review, the integrated body passes the full gate and the journeys below on the installed candidate, and its pull request to main is ready for a human merge.

The record’s summary, whole

Issue 272 asked for an orchestrator follow-up ledger: every handed-over item logged, checked and closed on proof. The operator shaped it on 2026-10-22 into project-level working state that CodeFlow owns for any orchestrating model, and an independent Codex review of the design (sound with changes, 22 findings, 14 high) settled its contracts: the coordination ledger, a clone-local single event log with follow-ups (FU-NNN, codeflow follow) and lanes (LN-NNN, codeflow lane), the coordinator as lead role, hooks on every harness, and the rules and skills that adopt them (ADR-0086). It is its own small epic, sized by issue 280's guidance, and it targets 3.2.0 as the operator placed issue 272 there. It lands on its own integration line, integration/EPC-025-the-coordination-ledger-follow-ups-and-lanes, cut from the EPC-022 line, because the epic-line binding (crates/codeflow-core/src/workgraph/work_start.rs:880-917) requires a task's epic to equal the line's epic, so an EPC-025 task cannot bind to the EPC-022 line (found at the first EPC-025 push on 2026-10-23; amended the same day, a reversible primary decision). The closing step: once its four tasks have landed and the epic's criteria are proven on its own installed candidate, the EPC-025 line merges into the EPC-022 line through one reviewed pull request, gated once as a candidate there, before the 3.2.0 pull request to main; that pull request describes both epics' outcomes, and the operator merges it. Amended 2026-10-24: codeflow ci lands an integration/ head only on the default branch, so each merge of this line into the EPC-022 line is carried by an EPC-022 task branch that merges it (the first is TSK-1000), and the operator chose that day to merge the line once now, with TSK-422 landed, so the 3.2.0 pull request can open.

TSK-397complete

After this merges, the strict text rule applies in every session by default.

The whole outcome, from the record

After this merges, the strict text rule applies in every session by default, and an operator can choose the line's rule for a project by landing `security.text_guard: relaxed` on its protected refs. No command the line refuses is allowed, except a line made only of bare `cd`, `pushd` and `popd` builtins under relaxed, which writes nothing. The change is breaking (4.0.0): `codeflow doctor --check sandbox` shows the rule in force.

The live journey of seat account profiles (TSK-431) needs your second Codex account

yours to clearopen since 12:11 EST, 2 Nov
  • Do: sign in a second Codex account and write accounts.toml in the root checkout
  • Why: decision d9 asks for the account proven live; no agent can sign in for you

The full recommendation and its source

Recommended: run mkdir -p ~/.codex-second, CODEX_HOME=~/.codex-second codex login, and create codeflow/.codeflow/local/accounts.toml in the root checkout; the Parallel Coordinator then starts the seat for AC-4.

Why: decision d9 (12:07 EST, 2 Nov) asks for the second account to be proven live, and no agent can sign in for you; checked 12:26 EST, 2 Nov: no ~/.codex-second, no file.

Alternative: accept AC-4 on the builder's recorded dry run instead, which records reduced assurance on the account-profile feature.

The installed hook binary was built from other hook and policy sources than the line

yours to clearunchanged since 2026-11-01
  • Do: rebuild the hook binary from the line, then rerun the gates
  • Why: the installed binary's source digest differs from the line's sources
  • Else: run the gates with the worktree binary first on PATH
The full recommendation and its source

Recommended: install the line's own build as the hook binary, or put the worktree's own build first on PATH for the lane, until 4.0.0 publishes. Not setting CODEFLOW_HOOK_BINARY is a relayed instruction from the Director (2 Nov), recorded here as relayed, not as a rule of the operating contract.

Why: every commit in this worktree printed codeflow judge: warning: built from different hook or policy sources; rebuild before trusting this judgment (12:33 EST, 2 Nov): the installed binary was built from other hook or policy sources than this worktree. The warning says only that; what each lane's gate judgment rests on is a separate question.

Alternative: keep 3.1.0 and put the worktree build first on PATH lane by lane, which repeats the workaround in every brief.

4 decisions for you

Each asks one question; the recommended answer is marked, never preselected; the Script view writes exactly what you chose.

1. The view tree: outcomes first, then the cross-cutting views
Context and why

The side menu's first area opens on the Overview and lists the three outcomes (one per epic); each opens to its themes (the epic's amendment sections) and each theme to its tasks. Epics, Lanes, Blockers, What changed, Evidence, Decisions, Script and Report kinds cut across.

Why: The theme level is the grouping the status facts command (TSK-1095 AC-15) already defines (the record section that introduced the task), so it costs nothing to compute and it keeps the 220-task list readable.

2. Tabs inside an outcome: Progress, Order, Issues
Context and why

Decision d2 chose three tabs per topic. The prototype shows Progress (percent, partition and themes), Order (the tasks in dependency order with their next-step reasons) and Issues (blocked, waiting and open pull requests for that epic).

Why: The three tabs answer the brief's questions 6, 3 and 4 inside one outcome without leaving it.

3. The task context strip: which facts lead
Context and why

A task view opens with a strip of labelled facts: outcome, location, lane, state, window, last moved, pull request (the status document, TSK-1098 AC-10). The prototype draws outcome, theme, location, state, record last changed and pull request; lane and window read not recorded until the status facts command (TSK-1095) lands them.

Why: The status facts command (TSK-1095 AC-15) says not recorded, never invented and never blank; the strip shows the rule.

4. Change marks since the previous report
Context and why

Numbers that moved since the report of 14:31 EST, 1 Nov carry a small delta beside them, and the menu dots the views with a change. Revision in place (TSK-1121) computes these from the previous revision of the same topic.

Why: An inline delta is the smallest mark that answers question 5 where the reader already is.

Docs portal/Git enforcement: the four planes

  
Git enforcement: the four planes
docs topic

  
  • Two planes are local: git hooks and in-session guards.
  • Two planes are the server-side boundary: scaffolded CI and remote branch protection.
  • All four read one policy file.
  • The guards are wired in each harness’s settings.
  • Remote protection is armed from the policy and read back by codeflow doctor.
CommandWhat it does
codeflow remote protectarms the remote plane where the host supports it
codeflow doctor --check remote-perimeterreads the live remote rules
codeflow cithe checks the hooks and CI share
